A bicycle gear system allows riders to adjust the resistance and speed of pedaling, making it easier to ride uphill or faster on flat terrain. The system consists of two main components: the front chainrings (attached to the pedals) and the rear cassette (attached to the rear wheel). These are connected by a chain that transfers power from the pedals to the rear wheel.

When you pedal, the chain moves across the chainrings and cassette, changing the gear ratio. The gear ratio is determined by dividing the number of teeth on the front chainring by the number of teeth on the rear cog. A higher ratio (larger front chainring or smaller rear cog) makes pedaling harder but moves the bike faster, ideal for downhill or flat rides.
